mechanisms.causalChain: A global risk shock or relative-yield change alters bilateral CHF demand; the exchange rate then changes foreign-currency revenue and input costs, importer prices, exporter markups and volumes, and monetary conditions. SNB FX intervention and policy rates can alter or lean against the move. The direction depends on the countercurrency and shock, not a single global CHF index.
mechanisms.counterEvidence: SNB safe-haven estimates find appreciation against EUR and carry currencies but depreciation against USD, JPY and GBP in stress; relationships vary over time. SNB reported a recent CHF depreciation supportive of exchange-sensitive exporters. The 2022 current-account paper finds headline current account largely inelastic at business-cycle frequency despite negative effects on exposed-sector profits and consumer prices. Latest SNB monthly averages for Sep 2026 (released 1 Oct) were CHF 0.94312/EUR and CHF 0.81926/USD; these levels alone do not establish appreciation over a chosen base, and the 2015 study finds bilateral rather than universal safe-haven behavior. In the 2015 synthetic-control study aggregate real export quantities were not significantly reduced despite about -7% short-run nominal CHF exports; pharma/chemicals and engineering/instruments differed.
mechanisms.stockFlowTransmission: Existing foreign-currency assets, liabilities, export receivables and imported-input payables revalue immediately; hedges, currency denomination and balance-sheet currency matching change the net cash effect. Price/volume and market-share flows respond over contracts, inventory and customer substitution horizons. A current-account balance is a flow, not a direct estimate of wealth or domestic output.
mechanisms.identificationLimits: Historical safe-haven regressions are currency-pair and sample dependent; common risk shocks confound bilateral exchange-rate moves. The 2015 policy discontinuity is unusually sharp and cannot identify every future shock. The current-account elasticity paper isolates exchange-rate variation but estimates aggregates that mask exposed sector profits, prices, gold trade and income offsets. A current bilateral monthly-average level is available, not a causal estimate; the 2015 floor-removal event is an unusually clean but one-off treatment. The 2025 synthetic-control study reports approximately 10% EUR appreciation, +8% nominal EUR exports over 18 months, around -7% nominal CHF exports short-run and insignificant aggregate real quantity response; counterfactual assumptions, short sample and lack of comparable sector quantity deflators constrain transfer.
mechanisms.modelability: Medium: scenario logic can use bilateral EUR/CHF and USD/CHF shocks, with separate unhedged exposures, import content and lagged price/volume channels. Calibrating future shock probabilities or a single economy-wide CHF elasticity is not warranted from these sources.
mechanisms.scenarioRelevance: High for a Swiss safe-haven branch: a sharp EUR appreciation of CHF can lower import inflation while compressing exporters' margins and output. Compare with SNB intervention, recent depreciation and non-EUR countercurrency paths.
mechanisms.unresolvedUncertainty: No verified current firm-level currency invoice, hedge maturity, pass-through, imported-input, foreign asset/liability or sector exposure matrix was assembled in this extraction. The sign and magnitude of a 2026–30 risk episode depend on risk source, yields, SNB actions and the bilateral currency involved.
mechanisms.investigationNotes: Investigated safe-haven direction, policy endogeneity, imported-input offsets, current-account aggregation and export-profit evidence. SNB Working Paper 2013-04 explicitly limits the safe-haven claim to some bilateral rates; SNB WP 2022-14 finds current-account inelasticity but confirms consumer prices and exposed-sector corporate profits decline after appreciation. Retain this mechanism but do not translate ‘anchor’ into universal appreciation or assume a current-account collapse. Collect 2026 bilateral effective rates, intervention/reserve data, exporter currency shares and sector hedges for later calibration. Targeted repair extracted SNB devkum September 2026 monthly averages directly from the official CSV endpoint (EUR1=0.94312 CHF; USD1=0.81926 CHF, publication timestamp 1 Oct 2026). These are monthly averages, not spot closing rates. Brunhart and Geiger (2025), synthetic control of customs exports Jan 2015–Jul 2017, estimate for roughly 10% EUR/CHF appreciation: nominal EUR exports +about 8% by 18 months, nominal CHF exports about -7% short term, and aggregate real quantities statistically indistinguishable from the counterfactual. Pharma/chemicals showed flexible prices and no significant real quantity loss; engineering and precision instruments suffered more. Data/code are on request and sectoral real deflators are unavailable, so no current elasticity is applied.

mechanisms.causalChain: CHF appreciation reduces the CHF price of foreign goods according to invoice currency and price-setting behavior; retailers and importers pass some change into consumer goods with lags. Energy, domestic services, rents, margins and the SNB policy response jointly determine CPI. CHF weakness or global commodity inflation can reverse the import disinflation contribution.
mechanisms.counterEvidence: 2015 transaction-level results show immediate complete pass-through for euro-invoiced imports and partial, rapid pass-through for CHF-invoiced goods, not full aggregate CPI pass-through. The 2007 VAR evidence finds import-price pass-through exceeds CPI pass-through and CPI sensitivity weakened in low/stable inflation. In September 2026 CPI inflation was 1.0% y/y, with SNB attributing the recent rise mainly to oil-product prices; the SNB forecast was revised higher partly due to energy and franc weakening. The September 2026 CHF exchange-rate level is not itself an import-price observation. SNB 2018 micro evidence around the >11% Jan 2015 shock found immediate, complete pass-through into euro-invoiced import unit values but only partial, exceptionally fast pass-through for CHF-invoiced goods (starting second working day and reaching medium-run pass-through after an average of 12 working days). Aggregate CPI pass-through is weaker in older VAR evidence; energy and administered prices can dominate monthly CPI. The latest FSO detailed import-price data available by 2026-10-14 cover August, while September CPI was 1.0% y/y. CPI release says heating oil, petrol and diesel rose, but this does not quantify an imported-goods CPI component or isolate CHF pass-through.
mechanisms.stockFlowTransmission: Exchange-rate changes reprice each period's import flow, while inventory contracts, retail pricing cycles and existing hedges delay cash and CPI effects. Lower import bills raise real household purchasing power and reduce input costs; they also affect nominal importer revenues and SNB real monetary conditions. CPI price level changes compound over time; monthly inflation is not the price-level effect itself.
mechanisms.identificationLimits: The 2015 event study uses daily transaction prices around a one-off floor removal and does not estimate the CPI basket response. The 1976–2004 VAR is dated and sensitive to recursive identification. Current CPI movements also reflect energy and domestic factors; forecast differences between SNB and SECO do not isolate CHF pass-through. FSO import-price index changes are measured series, not causal estimates of CHF appreciation effects; CPI narrative component directions are not a numeric import-only contribution. Release for September import prices post-dates the 2026-10-14 cutoff.
mechanisms.modelability: Medium: distinguish import prices by invoicing from aggregate CPI; use explicit shock scenarios and bounded pass-through/lag parameters. Treat SECO and SNB published inflation forecasts as conditional benchmarks, not causal coefficients or model estimates.
mechanisms.scenarioRelevance: High for consumer purchasing power and SNB branch logic. The user's 0.6% 2026–27 hypothesis matches SECO's September forecast exactly, but SNB's 24 September conditional forecast is 0.7%/0.8% and September CPI was 1.0% y/y; display this uncertainty and vintage distinction.
mechanisms.unresolvedUncertainty: Quantified September 2026 import price index is not available at cutoff (scheduled publication 2026-10-15); separate imported-goods CPI component values and firm-specific invoice currency/hedge pass-through are not in the archived located sources.
mechanisms.investigationNotes: The latest verified inflation observation in this pass is September 2026, released 1 October: CPI index 101.5 (Dec 2025=100), +1.0% y/y and flat m/m. SECO forecast published 17 September averages 0.6% for 2026 and 2027, finalized 8 September; SNB published 24 September conditional forecast averages 0.7%, 0.8% assuming 0% policy rate. Thus 0.6% is an official forecast but not a realized outcome or consensus. SNB's 2015 invoice-currency study and older VAR constrain pass-through rather than justify arbitrary full CPI response. Researched the empirical pass-through evidence rather than carrying forward a blanket appreciation-to-inflation multiplier: Bonadio, Fischer and Sauré (SNB WP 2018-05) use daily transaction-level import data around the 15 Jan 2015 policy discontinuity; complete and immediate response for euro-invoiced import unit values; partial fast response for CHF-invoiced goods from working day 2 and medium-run response after 12 working days on average. Historical event and invoice-currency split do not identify current CPI elasticity. Latest level evidence: September 2026 monthly-average CHF rates in SNB cube devkum. A current import-price/CPI-component pass-through panel remains unextracted; no current numerical coefficient assumed. RR0-CH-01 now links August 2026 detailed FSO import-price index rows (total and organic chemical category) and September CPI headline plus its dated component narrative. IPI index changes are computed from the underlying index levels and not treated as CPI effects.

mechanisms.causalChain: Foreign demand, regulatory access, product mix and CHF valuation affect high-value chemical/pharmaceutical export receipts; imported inputs, global pricing, local production, hedges and intellectual-property rents affect domestic value added. A temporary output or inventory shift can swing quarterly GDP and customs totals without indicating durable economy-wide demand.
mechanisms.counterEvidence: Q2 2026 growth was broad-based, and both SECO and SNB note that unusually high chemical/pharma value added made headline GDP overstate underlying momentum; SECO expected a second-half correction. Record exports are nominal goods totals and can reflect prices, product mix, shipment timing and foreign-produced goods rather than real Swiss value added. Current export totals are nominal gross customs flows. FOCBS Annex Ia establishes the 2026-Q1 chemical/pharmaceutical export level at CHF 33,652m and a seasonally adjusted nominal 8.1% q/q decline versus 2025-Q4 (CHF 2,959m) and Q2 2026 GDP contribution reversal risk temper the resilience interpretation. The 2015 study is a one-off event and real quantity resilience is not proof of profit or domestic value-added stability.
mechanisms.stockFlowTransmission: Export orders and shipments are quarterly flows against accumulated capacity, patents, production networks and inventories. CHF movements revalue foreign revenue and imported inputs; capacity/utilization and investment are stocks that adjust slowly. Domestic wages, supplier purchases, R&D and tax receipts transmit output changes into local income and future capacity.
mechanisms.identificationLimits: National accounts sector value added and customs merchandise exports measure different things and cannot be directly equated. No 2026 firm microdata on CHF exposure, transfer pricing, real export volumes, inventory, plant utilization or sectoral profits was available in accepted sources. 2015 sector responses do not identify 2026 elasticity. Annex Ia fixes the Q1 comparison basis as q/q and seasonally adjusted nominal. The customs value does not identify bilateral market-access effects or the causal exchange-rate contribution.
mechanisms.modelability: Medium with sector-level GDP contributions, export demand, imported content, price/volume split and an explicit transitory-volatility adjustment. Company financials and utilization are required before modeling firm margins or capex.
mechanisms.scenarioRelevance: High as a Swiss relative-anchor counterweight and a concentration risk: pharma/chemicals can buffer external weakness, but a volatile sector drove nearly half of exceptional Q2 sport-adjusted growth.
mechanisms.unresolvedUncertainty: Latest detailed official FOCBS yearbook sector result located is CHF 149.1bn and 52.7% of total exports in 2024; 2025 industry association using Swiss-Impex reports CHF 152.1bn (+2.2%) and >52%, but the exact 2025 detailed official customs yearbook table was not located. Q1 2026 decline is summarized by Confederation portal from FOCBS; download the underlying FOCBS data for independent replication. Real volume/price/product mix, firm FX hedges, utilization, sector value added and export margins are still unmeasured here.
mechanisms.investigationNotes: Official FOCBS release dated 29 January 2026 reports 2025 exports CHF 287.0bn (+1.4%), imports CHF 232.7bn (+4.5%) and CHF 54.3bn surplus. SECO Q2 national-accounts release dated 3 September gives 1.5% sport-event-adjusted q/q growth, after 0.5% prior quarter, and integrates revised annual data from 25 August. SECO says nearly half of Q2 increase came from volatile chemical/pharma value added; SNB characterizes growth as exceptionally strong but capacity use below average particularly in manufacturing. Don't treat recent growth as robust trend or sector nominal export totals as an elasticity. Repair adds FOCBS 2024 official yearbook figures (CHF 149.1bn, 52.7% of customs exports) and scienceindustries Jan 2026 Swiss-Impex-sourced preliminary 2025 sector figures (CHF 152.1bn, +2.2%, >52%, explicitly classified as an industry-association release), plus Federal Confederation portal summary and FOCBS Annex Ia for Q1 2026 chemical/pharma exports (-8.1%, CHF 2.959bn decline, seasonally adjusted nominal q/q vs 2025-Q4). Official FOCBS and SNB series report nominal customs or value-added units; do not infer real output. The 2015 sector study finds high-margin pharma/chemistry adjusted prices so real quantities were virtually unaffected, whereas mechanical engineering and precision instruments had larger adverse effects. RR0-CH-01 corrected the period conflict from the archived Annex Ia (PDF p.6 / printed p.5): CHF 33,652m, -8.1% nominal q/q SA vs 2025-Q4. Current FSO import-price detail now covers Aug 2026 total and organic chemical indices; these are price-index observations, not CHF pass-through estimates.

mechanisms.causalChain: Global commodity prices, trade finance, sanctions and counterparty risk affect Swiss merchanting turnover and margins; transactions can alter gross cross-border goods flows and the current account although goods are bought and resold abroad. Margins, services, employment and local taxes are the domestic transmission; financing and collateral links can amplify global liquidity stress.
mechanisms.counterEvidence: Merchanting is economically real Swiss-resident intermediation and can support domestic income, expertise, employment and services. However, gross trade flows are not domestic value added; commodity prices and gold can move external accounts without comparable Swiss production. Official SECO work highlights classification gaps and wide ranges in sector contribution estimates. In Q2 2026 the aggregate net current-account surplus was CHF 23.658bn while gross merchanting sales were CHF 238.247bn; the SNB text says the merchanting balance increased materially y/y but does not give its value. These must not be equated.
mechanisms.stockFlowTransmission: Current-account merchanting balance and financial-account settlement are flows; trade receivables, inventories held abroad, credit lines, collateral and foreign subsidiaries are balance-sheet stocks. A funding haircut or counterparty default can force working-capital drawdowns, reduce merchanting margins and trigger asset/liability retrenchment. Gross turnover should never enter Swiss GDP directly. Publicly extracted Q2 flows now separate gross merchanting turnover from the aggregate net current-account balance. Firm trade receivables, payables, FX hedges, counterparties, credit lines and collateral remain balance-sheet stocks not reported in these public tables.
mechanisms.identificationLimits: The sector is not cleanly classified in standard business statistics and contemporary firm-specific employment/value added/funding exposure is not present in the sources. Q2 BOP increases have low 2025 comparator and non-monetary gold effects. Historical cross-country merchanting results are not a Swiss current causal estimate. The SNB aggregate current-account cube does not isolate merchanting and the gross sales cube does not disclose purchases/net margin. No bilateral CHF/GDP effect can be identified from these national aggregates; 2015 event-study coefficients are not transported to current GDP forecasts.
mechanisms.modelability: Low to medium until merchanting margin, domestic service input, trade-finance maturity/collateral and counterparty data are available. BOP flow and IIP stock can be tracked as context; use explicit ranges for local value added, never turnover as GDP.
mechanisms.scenarioRelevance: Medium-high: the Swiss external surplus may appear as a resilience signal while financial-flow reversals or commodity trading distort measured goods balance. Stress trade-credit funding and global risk separately from domestic production.
mechanisms.unresolvedUncertainty: Exact 2026-Q2 net merchanting balance, merchanting value added/earnings retained domestically, trade-finance stocks, counterparty concentration, hedging and collateral exposures remain undisclosed in the located public sources.
mechanisms.investigationNotes: SNB Q2 2026 BOP release (22 Sep) reports a CHF 24bn current-account balance, up CHF 13bn y/y because goods trade increased; merchanting balance rose and non-monetary-gold balance was less negative, while services and income changed marginally. Financial-account transactions had net reductions in financial assets (CHF 6bn) and liabilities (CHF 12bn); N-IIP stood CHF 986bn, up CHF 22bn, largely market valuation. This is not evidence of outward capital flight: resident investors selling foreign shares and foreign parents withdrawing equity coexist with asset/liability reductions and reinvested earnings. SNB's merchanting definition excludes goods entering Switzerland/Liechtenstein. The 2018 SECO assessment is dated, classification-limited and should not anchor a current sector GDP share. Repair queried the SNB merchanting sales cube bopmercatq, latest release dated 22 Sep 2026. Total gross sales of goods (GT) in 2026-Q2 were CHF 238,247.4 million. This gross turnover series is distinct from merchanting balance/current-account margin and domestic value added; Q2 release separately reports CHF 24bn total current-account balance and states merchanting balance rose materially y/y but gives no exact merchanting balance in narrative. Gross sales magnitude is informative about flow scale, not GDP or domestic financing risk. SNB says transaction data revisions extend back to 2023. Closure RR0-CH-01 checked SNB bopmercatq (gross sales), bopoverq (net total current account) and Q2 release. Three likely net-cube endpoints bopmerchq, bopmerq and bopmerch returned HTTP 404; no merchanting-only amount was invented. The SNB release states the balance increased significantly versus 2025-Q2 but omits its amount. Q2 gross sales were CHF 238,247.4m; current-account net total was CHF 23,657.6m.

mechanisms.causalChain: Regulatory divergence, mutual-recognition coverage and institutional uncertainty affect fixed costs, certification, supply chains and investment for Swiss firms selling into the EU; a negotiated package may reduce some frictions after ratification, implementation and entry into force. Existing sector-specific discontinuities make the channel credible but do not quantify whole-economy costs.
mechanisms.counterEvidence: Switzerland retains substantial bilateral trade and firms can adapt, diversify markets or absorb compliance expense; some agreements and transitional arrangements continue. The 2026 package is signed and under parliamentary/democratic and EU procedures, so anticipated market-access improvements are not current realized conditions. Medical-device MRA is a bounded sector-specific example, not a measure of economy-wide loss.
mechanisms.stockFlowTransmission: Institutional status affects expected future market-access rents and investment decisions (capital stock), while border, certification and compliance costs affect current operating margins and trade flows. Ratification risk can defer capex or induce duplicate production/certification capacity. A legal milestone changes option value before any measured trade-flow response.
mechanisms.identificationLimits: No causal estimate isolates status-quo erosion from exchange rates, demand, product regulation, Brexit, US tariffs or firm selection. Framework agreement impacts depend on component text, implementation schedules, Swiss law and referendum results; no general effective date is established in reviewed official sources.
mechanisms.modelability: Medium as a conditional legal-status branch, with binary/dated implementation milestones and sensitivity ranges for market-access cost or investment response rather than a point GDP forecast. Identify implemented components separately from signed-but-not-effective agreements.
mechanisms.scenarioRelevance: High for a Swiss relative-anchor narrative: export concentration and uncertain EU rules can be downside channels, while an implemented package can support investment and participation. The two branches should not be conflated.
mechanisms.unresolvedUncertainty: As of 14 October 2026, need exact parliamentary timetable/votes, referendum trigger and timing, EU approval/ratification sequence, effective dates by component and firm-level estimates of lost or regained market access. Whether any package component entered into force after the dated updates needs source refresh before modeling.
mechanisms.investigationNotes: Verified the user-referenced ‘March 2026 package’: official FDFA tracker records remaining agreements signed 2 March; 13 March dispatch went to Parliament. The living FDFA page has 12 August status updates and contentious issues including electricity details; signatures do not equal ratification. The agreement on participation in EU programmes is a distinct early component signed 10 Nov 2025 and the SERI page says it applies immediately/retroactively from 1 Jan 2025. This program association does not mean the whole Bilaterals III package is effective. The EU medical-device MRA notice is a concrete historical access disruption; treat it as mechanism evidence, not a current aggregate GDP coefficient. Cutoff verification: FDFA records the remaining agreements signed 2 March 2026 and the Federal Council dispatch adopted/submitted to both chambers on 13 March; its latest dated political-status items located in this review are 12 August 2026, including referendum-design debate. These steps establish signature and parliamentary consideration, not Swiss ratification, EU conclusion or an effective date. As of the 14 October 2026 research cutoff, no general entry-into-force date is established in the reviewed official material. The 2021 medical-device MRA lapse remains a sector-specific precedent only.

mechanisms.causalChain: Physical electricity interconnection and research networks connect Switzerland to EU markets. Without legal guarantees and full institutional participation, cross-border scheduling/trading, system balancing and research collaboration face uncertainty; an electricity agreement can improve security, trading and grid stability, while programme-specific research association restores eligibility subject to call rules and financing.
mechanisms.counterEvidence: Swiss grids and researchers remain connected through physical links, national funding, bilateral cooperation and transitional measures; lacking a comprehensive agreement does not imply no cross-border electricity trade or research. Horizon programme association already applies from 2025 under a separate signed EUPA, and 2026–27 strategic access has call-specific restrictions/exceptions. Electricity package agreement is signed but in parliamentary phase.
mechanisms.stockFlowTransmission: Electricity reliability and market coupling affect operating cost, investment and capacity availability over time; congestion/capacity and generation assets are stocks, while imports, exports, balancing and prices are flows. Research access raises expected collaboration and grant flows and can accumulate knowledge/capital, with lags; eligibility is not equivalent to funded project output.
mechanisms.identificationLimits: Prospective agreement benefit is not yet an observed treatment effect; grid outcomes depend on weather, generation mix, interconnectors and neighbors. Horizon association cannot be evaluated from status alone; project awards and realized Swiss contributions/outcomes are required. Future effective dates cannot be inferred from signature.
mechanisms.modelability: Medium-low in current stage: legal status can be represented discretely, while economic benefits need power-flow/capacity models, price and outage data, and research call-level funding data. Avoid unsupported quantified multipliers.
mechanisms.scenarioRelevance: Medium-high: electricity price/security and access to Horizon Europe, Euratom and Digital Europe can differentiate Swiss outcomes under European fragmentation and friendshoring. Separate electricity from research agreement branches.
mechanisms.unresolvedUncertainty: Need latest parliamentary and referendum status, actual electricity-agreement effective date, dispatchability/cross-border capacity allocation under proposed rules, Swiss grid reliability/cost data, Horizon awards/participation by call and exceptions, and future Erasmus+/ITER/EU4Health access status.
mechanisms.investigationNotes: SFOE official page says Switzerland is physically/geographically closely integrated but lacks legal guarantees; the 2 March 2026 signature followed by dispatch to Parliament means proposed security-of-supply/trading benefits remain prospective. SERI states programme agreement signed 10 November 2025 applies immediately, associating Switzerland retroactively from 1 January 2025 to Horizon Europe, Euratom and Digital Europe; Commission validation then granted access to strategic Horizon 2026–27 calls including AI/quantum, with some space calls still excluded. Keep implementation, eligibility and funding as separate observable steps rather than treating access as enacted for every project or conferring general EU market access. Status is component-specific: SFOE confirms physical integration without legal guarantees and says the electricity agreement signed on 2 March 2026 entered the parliamentary phase after the March dispatch; no effective date is specified there. Separately, SERI states the EUPA was signed 10 November 2025 and applies immediately, retroactively associating Switzerland from 1 January 2025 to Horizon Europe, Euratom and Digital Europe. SERI reports full access to strategic Horizon 2026–27 calls after Commission validation, while certain space calls remain inaccessible; Digital Europe strategic calls were opened earlier but DEP Objectives 3 (cybersecurity) and 6 (semiconductors) are exceptions. Do not combine programme eligibility with package-wide legal force or electricity-market access.

mechanisms.causalChain: Geopolitical fragmentation or supply restrictions can lead Swiss firms to diversify suppliers, inventories, production locations and customer markets toward trusted partners. Diversification can improve resilience but may increase costs, reduce scale economies or simply relocate concentration; openness and EU market access shape feasible options.
mechanisms.counterEvidence: OECD review highlights resilience and diversification tradeoffs; Switzerland's strong export performance and open international networks indicate that global integration remains a source of specialization and demand, not just vulnerability. No verified Swiss causal estimate shows friendshoring net benefits, and recent CHF/export and pharma output swings show non-supply channels can dominate. OECD’s measured structural evidence offers concrete counterweight to a generic vulnerability story: average Swiss import HHI fell 7% from 2002 to 2021; high-concentration imports accounted for a lower share than in early 2000s; Swiss foreign-input reliance is below OECD average across most sectors. At the same time, EU suppliers provided 54% and Asian suppliers 17% of imported intermediate inputs on average (2018 data), and about 60 product-country combinations remained flagged in 2021. Relocation claims must distinguish diversified sourcing and EU dependence from actual nearshoring. The OECD September 2026 Switzerland Survey says Switzerland weathered recent shocks comparatively well, while remaining vulnerable to international trade/geopolitical uncertainty. This current qualitative assessment supports resilience and exposure together, but is not a causal estimate of friendshoring.
mechanisms.stockFlowTransmission: Supplier/customer concentration, inventories, production capacity, specialized labor and FDI are stocks; orders, imports, exports, inventory replenishment, investment and earnings are flows. Diversification requires upfront capital and may lower short-run productivity while reducing tail loss from disruption. Financial-account FDI and portfolio transactions cannot be treated as physical supply relocation without company-level evidence. OECD import HHI/product-country flags and TiVA foreign-input shares map supplier concentration and upstream stocks; changes in sourcing, inventory, output, and investment are flows. OECD documents some Swiss firms sourcing critical Chinese inputs shifting purchases toward Europe or own European production, but this dated evidence is not a whole-economy friendshoring flow measure.
mechanisms.identificationLimits: Friendshoring is inconsistently defined and confounded by tariffs, exchange rates, demand, regulation, firm strategy and pandemic-era inventory shifts. OECD material is primarily pre-2024 and does not estimate a 2026–30 counterfactual. Swiss current-account and IIP changes do not reveal supplier relocation or FDI motives. OECD 2024 reports data mainly through 2018–2021: imported intermediates averaged 54% EU, 17% Asia, 10% North America, 8% rest of Europe and 11% other; average import HHI fell 7% from 2002 to 2021 and about 60 high-risk country-product pairs remained flagged in 2021. The data indicate concentration/diversification, not changes caused by friendshoring. A planned nearshoring survey found in trade press/industry sources is not used as national evidence.
mechanisms.modelability: Low to medium until firm-level supplier origin/concentration, inventory, input-output exposure, logistics and substitution times are assembled. A scenario can bound disruption/reallocation costs and resilience benefits, but should label them assumptions and avoid a single net friendshoring coefficient.
mechanisms.scenarioRelevance: Medium: trusted-partner access may support Switzerland as a relative anchor, while concentrated pharmaceutical/chemical exports, EU market-access uncertainty, commodity trading and energy dependence expose it to geopolitical shocks.
mechanisms.unresolvedUncertainty: Current 2022–26 product-level import concentration, input origin at firm level, critical-input inventories, substitution lags, FDI plant relocation and whether the EU share reflects resilience or concentration remain unknown. OECD’s 2018 input-output/2002–21 customs results are the strongest public structural baseline found; this repair does not claim a causal net friendshoring return.
mechanisms.investigationNotes: Investigated diversification as a conditional resilience channel rather than an observed Swiss structural break. OECD's 2024 GVC and EU-integration analyses supply the strongest broader evidence and counterevidence, but predate recent legal milestones and do not quantify causal gains. SNB Q2 2026 external accounts show large balance-sheet transactions and valuation changes; they are not measures of production relocation. Later work should combine Swiss input-output tables with customs origin/use detail, sector-specific supplier mapping and dated legal access status, separating concentration risk from foreign-exchange and export-demand shocks. Deepened investigation using OECD Switzerland 2024, its cited CEPII product-level dependency screen and OECD TiVA-based input reliance. Figure 5.10 reports imported intermediate input suppliers averaging EU 54%, Asia 17%, North America 10%, rest Europe 8%, other 11% (2018). Text reports about 60 country-product combinations still at risk two years after the 2019 screen (through 2021), using import HHI>0.4, global export HHI>0.4 and import value greater than exports. Figure 5.12 reports mean import HHI fell 7% 2002–2021 and high-concentration import share fell since early 2000s. OECD documents some surveyed Swiss companies reduced critical China sourcing mainly through more European purchases and to lesser extent EU production/process adaptation (Eichenauer & Domjahn 2023), but no causal economy-wide net effect. These lagged data are source-linked baseline exposure evidence; refresh is required before asserting present 2026 supplier mix. Also checked the latest OECD Switzerland Survey (15 Sep 2026): its summary finds the economy weathered recent shocks comparatively well but remains vulnerable to international trade/geopolitical uncertainty and emphasizes strong trading ties and market expansion. It has no causal friendshoring coefficient in the reviewed summary; deeper quantified sourcing metrics still rely on OECD 2024 vintages.
